title: Harness Engineering: How to Build Software When Humans Steer, Agents Execute — Ryan Lopopolo, OpenAI
talk_summary: Ryan Lopopolo describes running a team that builds software exclusively through coding agents, treating code as a free, disposable artifact and focusing human effort on encoding 'what good looks like' into the repo. The core mechanism is converting recurring human review feedback into durable, machine-readable guardrails (docs, custom lints, source-structure tests, persona review agents) that just-in-time prompt-inject agents so they self-heal.

takeaways.technique: Persona-bucketed review agents fed by documented standards
takeaways.what_they_do: Bucket human review feedback by persona (frontend architect, reliability, scalability), write down what good looks like per persona, then run a review agent on every push that surfaces P2+ blockers against those docs.
takeaways.evidence_quote: for each of those personas, we spun up a review agent that gets triggered on every push that says, 'Is this code good?'

takeaways.technique: Source-structure tests and bespoke lints as prompt injection
takeaways.what_they_do: Write tests/lints that assert properties of the source itself (file length limits, no duplicate schemas, single canonical helper, retry+timeout around fetch) with error messages that tell the agent the remediation step.
takeaways.evidence_quote: we can write a test that limits the fact that files are no longer than 350 lines

takeaways.technique: Just-in-time instruction surfacing instead of front-loading
takeaways.what_they_do: Don't dump all requirements up front; let the agent prototype, then surface constraints at lint/test/review time so the agent revises the patch before merge.
takeaways.evidence_quote: let the agent cook and prototype... And then at lint or test time, say, 'Okay, you've done the work. In order to finish it, you have to break this apart'

takeaways.technique: Garbage-collection day to convert review feedback into guardrails
takeaways.what_they_do: Reserve recurring time where the whole team takes the week's review slop and builds categorical fixes (docs, lints, reviewer agents) so the same feedback never recurs.
takeaways.evidence_quote: take every bit of slop we had observed over the course of the week... figure out ways to categorically eliminate it from ever happening

takeaways.technique: Treat 'continue' prompts as harness failures; define work so agents run to completion
takeaways.what_they_do: Skills tell the agent to run until tests are green; the goal is many agents running unattended with no human button-pressing.
takeaways.evidence_quote: Every time I have to type continue to the agent is like a failure of the harness to provide enough context around what it means to continue

takeaways.technique: Few centralized skills hiding churning tooling
takeaways.what_they_do: Keep 5-10 skills and improve them rather than proliferating; hide frequently-changing dev tooling beneath stable skill interfaces so agents adapt without humans tracking changes.
takeaways.evidence_quote: we kind of centralize our leverage around five to 10 skills... preferring to make the existing skills better
